solution: Destination can observe a mixed value that never existed at the source; independent bit synchronizers do not establish bus coherence.
For occasional snapshots, hold the data stable while a synchronized handshake controls capture and acknowledgment. For streaming data, use an asynchronous FIFO with a proven CDC implementation.

Gray-coded pointer crossings can help FIFO control because adjacent pointer codes differ by one bit, but still require synchronizers, physical bus-skew/delay constraints and correct pointer/full-empty logic.
rubric: Explains incoherent multi-bit capture
Gives snapshot and streaming solutions
Does not claim Gray code alone solves all CDC issues
followups: Why can Gray bits still fail if their physical delays differ too much?
Can you safely cross arbitrary payload data by Gray-encoding it?
theory: Timing exceptions do not create synchronization hardware.
CDC methodology must include implementation constraints as well as RTL.

title: Ready/valid buffer under backpressure
prompt: Implement a one-entry elastic register. It must hold output data stable while stalled, accept a replacement in the same cycle as a dequeue, and clear valid on reset. Assume synchronous active-high reset and no combinational ready loop outside the module.
artifact:
SYNTHETIC PRACTICE FIXTURE — not a tool run or foundry data
Inputs: clk, rst, in_valid, in_data[7:0], out_ready
Outputs: in_ready, out_valid, out_data[7:0]
Transfer = valid && ready at rising edge
No requirement to clear payload bits on reset
hint: The slot can accept when it is empty or when its old item is being consumed.
solution: Set in_ready = !out_valid || out_ready.
On reset clear out_valid. Otherwise, when in_ready, load out_valid from in_valid and capture payload if in_valid. When blocked, preserve both valid and payload.

title: Size the signed accumulator before coding
prompt: Derive the minimum signed accumulator width for an exact sum of 16 products of signed 8-bit operands. No saturation or truncation is allowed.
artifact:
SYNTHETIC PRACTICE FIXTURE — not a tool run or foundry data
a,b ∈ [−128,127]
acc = Σ(a[i] × b[i]), i=0..15
A proposed accumulator is signed [18:0] (19 bits)
hint: The largest positive product is (−128)×(−128), not 127×127.
solution: One product ranges from −16,256 to +16,384 and fits signed 16 bits.
The sum ranges from −260,096 to +262,144. Signed 19-bit maximum is +262,143, so the proposed width fails by one at the positive extreme; 20 bits is sufficient.
Declare operands/intermediates signed, preserve full product precision, and sign-extend before addition. Include all −128 operands and mixed-sign extrema in testing.
rubric: Finds the positive extreme correctly
Derives 20-bit width rather than guessing
Handles signedness and extreme-value tests
followups: Would unsigned 8×8 need the same sum width?
How would saturation change the output contract?
theory: Range analysis should precede arithmetic implementation.
Expression sizing and signed casts can affect RTL behavior.

title: Assert stability during backpressure
prompt: Write an assertion for a synchronous ready/valid source. If valid is high and ready low at a sampled edge, the next sampled edge must still have valid high and the same data. Reset cancels the check.
artifact:
SYNTHETIC PRACTICE FIXTURE — not a tool run or foundry data
Signals: clk, rst_n, valid, ready, data[31:0]
Source cannot withdraw a pending item
The next cycle may complete the transfer
hint: Use a next-cycle implication. Require stable data even if ready becomes high on that next edge.
solution: Use a non-overlapped implication from valid && !ready to valid && $stable(data), disabled during reset.
A correct checker catches withdrawal and payload mutation. Add a cover for a stall followed by acceptance to ensure useful stimulus.
This property does not prove correct payload values, no duplication, or eventual readiness; those need separate checks and assumptions.

Explains what the assertion does not prove

title: The scoreboard accepted a dropped packet
prompt: Find why the test passed and design stronger completion checks. The DUT is an in-order packet transformer.
artifact:
SYNTHETIC PRACTICE FIXTURE — not a tool run or foundry data
Inputs accepted: 100
Expected queue pushes: 100
Outputs observed and compared: 99
All 99 comparisons match
Test ends after fixed 1,000 cycles
Scoreboard reports PASS because mismatch_count == 0
hint: Correct observed outputs do not prove every required output arrived.
solution: One expected transaction remains unmatched. The checker only detects wrong outputs that actually arrive.
Require expected queue drained, expected/actual counts consistent, no unexpected outputs, and a bounded completion timeout based on the protocol. Flag leftover transactions at end of test.
Build expected items from accepted inputs, observe actual outputs independently, and verify ordering/IDs as required. Test dropped, duplicated, reordered and corrupted outcomes.

Keeps predictor independent of DUT results

theory: A scoreboard needs both comparison and completion semantics.
Timeout assumptions belong in the test contract.

title: A random failure needs a reproducible story
prompt: Outline a debug sequence and the minimal replay record. Do not “fix” the test by deleting the failing seed.
